questions.q: What is the main purpose of the Brookside roof project?
questions.a: To replace science lessons with gardening
questions.b: To build a decorative park for visitors
questions.c: To create a local learning project that also responds to heat and water concerns
questions.d: To prove that air conditioning is unnecessary
questions.passage:
When Brookside Secondary School replaced a section of its dark roof with a garden, the project began as a practical response to summer heat. The building’s top floor had become uncomfortable by early afternoon, and the air-conditioning system was working harder each year. Teachers proposed a green roof: a shallow layer of soil and hardy plants installed over a waterproof membrane. The school also added rain barrels and a small weather station so pupils could study the changes rather than simply admire the plants.

The first results were modest but measurable. On hot days, the roof surface beneath the plants was cooler than the exposed section. Classrooms directly below the garden warmed more slowly, although the effect varied with wind, cloud cover and how wet the soil was. The school therefore avoided claiming that the garden alone had solved its energy problem. Instead, science classes compared temperature readings across several months and discussed which other factors might explain the pattern.

Rainwater collection produced a second benefit. Water from the barrels was used for the garden, reducing the amount taken from the school supply during dry weeks. Pupils noticed that a heavy storm filled the barrels quickly, while a series of light showers did not. They used these observations to estimate water use and to consider why storage capacity matters in cities where paved surfaces send rain into drains rather than soil.

The project also changed how lessons were organized. Biology classes recorded plant growth, mathematics groups calculated averages, and English learners wrote short reports for families. A local horticulturist advised the school to choose native plants that could survive periods without watering. This advice challenged the assumption that a roof garden should look like a decorative park. The goal was resilience and learning, not a perfect display.

Brookside’s experience cannot be copied exactly everywhere. Roof strength, climate, maintenance budgets and access to water differ from school to school. The staff now share their measurements and mistakes with neighboring schools, emphasizing that a useful climate project begins with a local question, gathers evidence over time and remains honest about uncertainty.

questions.q: At gap G2, which sentence best introduces success criteria?
questions.a: For this reason, students should never revise a draft.
questions.b: These criteria make the target visible before the work is assessed.
questions.c: The roof garden provides a useful example of rainfall.
questions.d: By contrast, spelling has no place in writing.
questions.passage:
Teachers often return marked work with the intention of helping learners improve. Yet a page covered in corrections may leave a student unsure where to begin. Feedback becomes more useful when it points to a manageable next step. [G1]

A learner who knows the goal can compare a draft with clear success criteria. [G2] For example, a writing task might ask students to support one claim with evidence and explain how the evidence relates to it. [G3] The teacher can then comment on that feature before addressing every spelling choice. [G4] Students need time to act on the comments, not merely read them. [G5]

A short revision cycle makes feedback part of learning rather than a final judgement. This approach does not mean that accuracy is unimportant. It means that comments should be prioritized. When a class is practicing past-tense narratives, repeated errors with verb forms may deserve attention; during a debate unit, clarity of reasoning may matter more. A teacher can also ask learners to identify one strength and one question about their own work. Such reflection helps them take responsibility without pretending that they can diagnose every problem alone.

Over time, teachers can review patterns across student work and adjust instruction. If many learners misunderstand the same feature, the next lesson can address it directly. In this way, assessment information guides both the learner’s revision and the teacher’s planning.

questions.q: What did the volunteer allow Malika to do?
questions.d: Borrow a notebook for a week
questions.passage:
On the first Monday of September, Malika opened the old English dictionary that had belonged to her grandfather. She was looking for the word “ordinary” because her new class had been asked to write about an ordinary object. A thin envelope slipped from between the pages and landed on the desk. Her name was written on it in her grandfather’s careful handwriting, though he had died before she started secondary school.

Inside was a note and a bus ticket from a town she had never visited. The note said that her grandfather had once missed an important interview because he was afraid to ask a stranger for directions. He had walked for an hour, arrived late and blamed the bus. “When you do not know a word or a way,” he wrote, “ask a question before the problem grows.” Malika laughed at the advice, then noticed a second line: the ticket was for the town library, where he had learned English as a young man.

That Saturday, she persuaded her mother to take her there. The library was smaller than she expected, but an elderly volunteer recognized the surname on the note. He showed Malika a shelf of old notebooks. Her grandfather had written unfamiliar words in the margins and added example sentences from conversations he heard at the market. Some spellings were wrong, and several pages were crossed out. Malika liked these mistakes more than the neat dictionary entries because they showed someone learning in real time.

The volunteer offered to let her borrow one notebook for a week. Malika chose the thinnest one and copied a phrase about asking for help into her own notebook. On the way home, the bus stopped at an unfamiliar street after a road closure. A passenger looked confused. This time Malika asked the driver which stop was nearest to the library. The answer saved them both a long walk.

For her class assignment, Malika wrote about the envelope, the notebook and the question she had asked on the bus. She concluded that an ordinary object can carry an unusual lesson, but only if someone is willing to open it.

questions.q: Why did Malika open the dictionary?
questions.a: She was looking for a bus timetable
questions.b: She needed the meaning of “ordinary” for a class assignment
questions.c: She wanted to find her grandfather’s address
questions.d: She was preparing a science report
questions.passage:
On the first Monday of September, Malika opened the old English dictionary that had belonged to her grandfather. She was looking for the word “ordinary” because her new class had been asked to write about an ordinary object. A thin envelope slipped from between the pages and landed on the desk. Her name was written on it in her grandfather’s careful handwriting, though he had died before she started secondary school.

Inside was a note and a bus ticket from a town she had never visited. The note said that her grandfather had once missed an important interview because he was afraid to ask a stranger for directions. He had walked for an hour, arrived late and blamed the bus. “When you do not know a word or a way,” he wrote, “ask a question before the problem grows.” Malika laughed at the advice, then noticed a second line: the ticket was for the town library, where he had learned English as a young man.

That Saturday, she persuaded her mother to take her there. The library was smaller than she expected, but an elderly volunteer recognized the surname on the note. He showed Malika a shelf of old notebooks. Her grandfather had written unfamiliar words in the margins and added example sentences from conversations he heard at the market. Some spellings were wrong, and several pages were crossed out. Malika liked these mistakes more than the neat dictionary entries because they showed someone learning in real time.

The volunteer offered to let her borrow one notebook for a week. Malika chose the thinnest one and copied a phrase about asking for help into her own notebook. On the way home, the bus stopped at an unfamiliar street after a road closure. A passenger looked confused. This time Malika asked the driver which stop was nearest to the library. The answer saved them both a long walk.

For her class assignment, Malika wrote about the envelope, the notebook and the question she had asked on the bus. She concluded that an ordinary object can carry an unusual lesson, but only if someone is willing to open it.

questions.q: Why did Malika like the crossed-out pages?
questions.a: They made the notebook easier to read
questions.b: They contained directions to the town
questions.c: They showed that her grandfather had learned through mistakes
questions.d: They proved the dictionary was inaccurate
questions.passage:
On the first Monday of September, Malika opened the old English dictionary that had belonged to her grandfather. She was looking for the word “ordinary” because her new class had been asked to write about an ordinary object. A thin envelope slipped from between the pages and landed on the desk. Her name was written on it in her grandfather’s careful handwriting, though he had died before she started secondary school.

Inside was a note and a bus ticket from a town she had never visited. The note said that her grandfather had once missed an important interview because he was afraid to ask a stranger for directions. He had walked for an hour, arrived late and blamed the bus. “When you do not know a word or a way,” he wrote, “ask a question before the problem grows.” Malika laughed at the advice, then noticed a second line: the ticket was for the town library, where he had learned English as a young man.

That Saturday, she persuaded her mother to take her there. The library was smaller than she expected, but an elderly volunteer recognized the surname on the note. He showed Malika a shelf of old notebooks. Her grandfather had written unfamiliar words in the margins and added example sentences from conversations he heard at the market. Some spellings were wrong, and several pages were crossed out. Malika liked these mistakes more than the neat dictionary entries because they showed someone learning in real time.

The volunteer offered to let her borrow one notebook for a week. Malika chose the thinnest one and copied a phrase about asking for help into her own notebook. On the way home, the bus stopped at an unfamiliar street after a road closure. A passenger looked confused. This time Malika asked the driver which stop was nearest to the library. The answer saved them both a long walk.

For her class assignment, Malika wrote about the envelope, the notebook and the question she had asked on the bus. She concluded that an ordinary object can carry an unusual lesson, but only if someone is willing to open it.

questions.q: At gap G2, which sentence best introduces success criteria?
questions.a: These criteria make the target visible before the work is assessed.
questions.b: By contrast, spelling has no place in writing.
questions.c: The roof garden provides a useful example of rainfall.
questions.d: For this reason, students should never revise a draft.
questions.passage:
Teachers often return marked work with the intention of helping learners improve. Yet a page covered in corrections may leave a student unsure where to begin. Feedback becomes more useful when it points to a manageable next step. [G1]

A learner who knows the goal can compare a draft with clear success criteria. [G2] For example, a writing task might ask students to support one claim with evidence and explain how the evidence relates to it. [G3] The teacher can then comment on that feature before addressing every spelling choice. [G4] Students need time to act on the comments, not merely read them. [G5]

A short revision cycle makes feedback part of learning rather than a final judgement. This approach does not mean that accuracy is unimportant. It means that comments should be prioritized. When a class is practicing past-tense narratives, repeated errors with verb forms may deserve attention; during a debate unit, clarity of reasoning may matter more. A teacher can also ask learners to identify one strength and one question about their own work. Such reflection helps them take responsibility without pretending that they can diagnose every problem alone.

Over time, teachers can review patterns across student work and adjust instruction. If many learners misunderstand the same feature, the next lesson can address it directly. In this way, assessment information guides both the learner’s revision and the teacher’s planning.

questions.q: What did Malika discover at the library?

questions.b: A dictionary with all the pages removed
questions.c: Her grandfather’s notebooks of new words and example sentences

He had walked for an hour, arrived late and blamed the bus. “When you do not know a word or a way,” he wrote, “ask a question before the problem grows.” Malika laughed at the advice, then noticed a second line: the ticket was for the town library, where he had learned English as a young man.

That Saturday, she persuaded her mother to take her there. The library was smaller than she expected, but an elderly volunteer recognized the surname on the note. He showed Malika a shelf of old notebooks. Her grandfather had written unfamiliar words in the margins and added example sentences from conversations he heard at the market. Some spellings were wrong, and several pages were crossed out. Malika liked these mistakes more than the neat dictionary entries because they showed someone learning in real time.

The volunteer offered to let her borrow one notebook for a week. Malika chose the thinnest one and copied a phrase about asking for help into her own notebook. On the way home, the bus stopped at an unfamiliar street after a road closure. A passenger looked confused. This time Malika asked the driver which stop was nearest to the library. The answer saved them both a long walk.

For her class assignment, Malika wrote about the envelope, the notebook and the question she had asked on the bus. She concluded that an ordinary object can carry an unusual lesson, but only if someone is willing to open it.

The building’s top floor had become uncomfortable by early afternoon, and the air-conditioning system was working harder each year. Teachers proposed a green roof: a shallow layer of soil and hardy plants installed over a waterproof membrane. The school also added rain barrels and a small weather station so pupils could study the changes rather than simply admire the plants.

The first results were modest but measurable. On hot days, the roof surface beneath the plants was cooler than the exposed section. Classrooms directly below the garden warmed more slowly, although the effect varied with wind, cloud cover and how wet the soil was. The school therefore avoided claiming that the garden alone had solved its energy problem. Instead, science classes compared temperature readings across several months and discussed which other factors might explain the pattern.

Rainwater collection produced a second benefit. Water from the barrels was used for the garden, reducing the amount taken from the school supply during dry weeks. Pupils noticed that a heavy storm filled the barrels quickly, while a series of light showers did not. They used these observations to estimate water use and to consider why storage capacity matters in cities where paved surfaces send rain into drains rather than soil.

The project also changed how lessons were organized. Biology classes recorded plant growth, mathematics groups calculated averages, and English learners wrote short reports for families. A local horticulturist advised the school to choose native plants that could survive periods without watering. This advice challenged the assumption that a roof garden should look like a decorative park. The goal was resilience and learning, not a perfect display.

Brookside’s experience cannot be copied exactly everywhere. Roof strength, climate, maintenance budgets and access to water differ from school to school. The staff now share their measurements and mistakes with neighboring schools, emphasizing that a useful climate project begins with a local question, gathers evidence over time and remains honest about uncertainty.

questions.q: What does her grandfather mean by “ask a question before the problem grows”?
questions.b: Avoid speaking to strangers in public
questions.c: Blame the bus when plans fail
questions.d: Seek help early when something is unclear
questions.passage:
On the first Monday of September, Malika opened the old English dictionary that had belonged to her grandfather. She was looking for the word “ordinary” because her new class had been asked to write about an ordinary object. A thin envelope slipped from between the pages and landed on the desk. Her name was written on it in her grandfather’s careful handwriting, though he had died before she started secondary school.

Inside was a note and a bus ticket from a town she had never visited. The note said that her grandfather had once missed an important interview because he was afraid to ask a stranger for directions. He had walked for an hour, arrived late and blamed the bus. “When you do not know a word or a way,” he wrote, “ask a question before the problem grows.” Malika laughed at the advice, then noticed a second line: the ticket was for the town library, where he had learned English as a young man.

That Saturday, she persuaded her mother to take her there. The library was smaller than she expected, but an elderly volunteer recognized the surname on the note. He showed Malika a shelf of old notebooks. Her grandfather had written unfamiliar words in the margins and added example sentences from conversations he heard at the market. Some spellings were wrong, and several pages were crossed out. Malika liked these mistakes more than the neat dictionary entries because they showed someone learning in real time.

The volunteer offered to let her borrow one notebook for a week. Malika chose the thinnest one and copied a phrase about asking for help into her own notebook. On the way home, the bus stopped at an unfamiliar street after a road closure. A passenger looked confused. This time Malika asked the driver which stop was nearest to the library. The answer saved them both a long walk.

For her class assignment, Malika wrote about the envelope, the notebook and the question she had asked on the bus. She concluded that an ordinary object can carry an unusual lesson, but only if someone is willing to open it.

questions.a: A map showing the bus route to her school
questions.b: A dictionary with all the pages removed
questions.c: Her grandfather’s notebooks of new words and example sentences
questions.d: A letter from her English teacher

questions.q: Why did the staff avoid saying that the garden alone solved the energy problem?
questions.a: Because pupils refused to take measurements
questions.b: Because weather and other conditions also affected the readings
questions.c: Because the air-conditioning system had been removed
questions.d: Because the garden had no plants
questions.passage:
When Brookside Secondary School replaced a section of its dark roof with a garden, the project began as a practical response to summer heat. The building’s top floor had become uncomfortable by early afternoon, and the air-conditioning system was working harder each year. Teachers proposed a green roof: a shallow layer of soil and hardy plants installed over a waterproof membrane. The school also added rain barrels and a small weather station so pupils could study the changes rather than simply admire the plants.

The first results were modest but measurable. On hot days, the roof surface beneath the plants was cooler than the exposed section. Classrooms directly below the garden warmed more slowly, although the effect varied with wind, cloud cover and how wet the soil was. The school therefore avoided claiming that the garden alone had solved its energy problem. Instead, science classes compared temperature readings across several months and discussed which other factors might explain the pattern.

Rainwater collection produced a second benefit. Water from the barrels was used for the garden, reducing the amount taken from the school supply during dry weeks. Pupils noticed that a heavy storm filled the barrels quickly, while a series of light showers did not. They used these observations to estimate water use and to consider why storage capacity matters in cities where paved surfaces send rain into drains rather than soil.

The project also changed how lessons were organized. Biology classes recorded plant growth, mathematics groups calculated averages, and English learners wrote short reports for families. A local horticulturist advised the school to choose native plants that could survive periods without watering. This advice challenged the assumption that a roof garden should look like a decorative park. The goal was resilience and learning, not a perfect display.

Brookside’s experience cannot be copied exactly everywhere. Roof strength, climate, maintenance budgets and access to water differ from school to school. The staff now share their measurements and mistakes with neighboring schools, emphasizing that a useful climate project begins with a local question, gathers evidence over time and remains honest about uncertainty.

questions.q: How did Malika apply the note’s advice on the bus?
questions.a: She waited for another passenger to speak
questions.b: She asked the driver which stop was nearest
questions.c: She walked until she recognized a street
questions.passage:
On the first Monday of September, Malika opened the old English dictionary that had belonged to her grandfather. She was looking for the word “ordinary” because her new class had been asked to write about an ordinary object. A thin envelope slipped from between the pages and landed on the desk. Her name was written on it in her grandfather’s careful handwriting, though he had died before she started secondary school.

Inside was a note and a bus ticket from a town she had never visited. The note said that her grandfather had once missed an important interview because he was afraid to ask a stranger for directions. He had walked for an hour, arrived late and blamed the bus. “When you do not know a word or a way,” he wrote, “ask a question before the problem grows.” Malika laughed at the advice, then noticed a second line: the ticket was for the town library, where he had learned English as a young man.

That Saturday, she persuaded her mother to take her there. The library was smaller than she expected, but an elderly volunteer recognized the surname on the note. He showed Malika a shelf of old notebooks. Her grandfather had written unfamiliar words in the margins and added example sentences from conversations he heard at the market. Some spellings were wrong, and several pages were crossed out. Malika liked these mistakes more than the neat dictionary entries because they showed someone learning in real time.

The volunteer offered to let her borrow one notebook for a week. Malika chose the thinnest one and copied a phrase about asking for help into her own notebook. On the way home, the bus stopped at an unfamiliar street after a road closure. A passenger looked confused. This time Malika asked the driver which stop was nearest to the library. The answer saved them both a long walk.

For her class assignment, Malika wrote about the envelope, the notebook and the question she had asked on the bus. She concluded that an ordinary object can carry an unusual lesson, but only if someone is willing to open it.

questions.q: At gap G4, which sentence best explains why feedback needs prioritizing?
questions.a: Students learn best when they receive no response.
questions.b: A long list of corrections is always easier to follow.
questions.c: Addressing one important feature can keep comments focused and usable.

questions.passage:
Teachers often return marked work with the intention of helping learners improve. Yet a page covered in corrections may leave a student unsure where to begin. Feedback becomes more useful when it points to a manageable next step. [G1]

A learner who knows the goal can compare a draft with clear success criteria. [G2] For example, a writing task might ask students to support one claim with evidence and explain how the evidence relates to it. [G3] The teacher can then comment on that feature before addressing every spelling choice. [G4] Students need time to act on the comments, not merely read them. [G5]

A short revision cycle makes feedback part of learning rather than a final judgement. This approach does not mean that accuracy is unimportant. It means that comments should be prioritized. A teacher can also ask learners to identify one strength and one question about their own work. Such reflection helps them take responsibility without pretending that they can diagnose every problem alone.

Over time, teachers can review patterns across student work and adjust instruction. If many learners misunderstand the same feature, the next lesson can address it directly. In this way, assessment information guides both the learner’s revision and the teacher’s planning.

questions.q: What did Malika discover at the library?
questions.a: A dictionary with all the pages removed
questions.b: A letter from her English teacher
questions.c: A map showing the bus route to her school
questions.d: Her grandfather’s notebooks of new words and example sentences
questions.passage:
On the first Monday of September, Malika opened the old English dictionary that had belonged to her grandfather. She was looking for the word “ordinary” because her new class had been asked to write about an ordinary object. A thin envelope slipped from between the pages and landed on the desk. Her name was written on it in her grandfather’s careful handwriting, though he had died before she started secondary school.

Inside was a note and a bus ticket from a town she had never visited. The note said that her grandfather had once missed an important interview because he was afraid to ask a stranger for directions. He had walked for an hour, arrived late and blamed the bus. “When you do not know a word or a way,” he wrote, “ask a question before the problem grows.” Malika laughed at the advice, then noticed a second line: the ticket was for the town library, where he had learned English as a young man.

That Saturday, she persuaded her mother to take her there. The library was smaller than she expected, but an elderly volunteer recognized the surname on the note. He showed Malika a shelf of old notebooks. Her grandfather had written unfamiliar words in the margins and added example sentences from conversations he heard at the market. Some spellings were wrong, and several pages were crossed out. Malika liked these mistakes more than the neat dictionary entries because they showed someone learning in real time.

The volunteer offered to let her borrow one notebook for a week. Malika chose the thinnest one and copied a phrase about asking for help into her own notebook. On the way home, the bus stopped at an unfamiliar street after a road closure. A passenger looked confused. This time Malika asked the driver which stop was nearest to the library. The answer saved them both a long walk.

For her class assignment, Malika wrote about the envelope, the notebook and the question she had asked on the bus. She concluded that an ordinary object can carry an unusual lesson, but only if someone is willing to open it.

On the first Monday of September, Malika opened the old English dictionary that had belonged to her grandfather. She was looking for the word “ordinary” because her new class had been asked to write about an ordinary object. A thin envelope slipped from between the pages and landed on the desk. Her name was written on it in her grandfather’s careful handwriting, though he had died before she started secondary school.

Inside was a note and a bus ticket from a town she had never visited. The note said that her grandfather had once missed an important interview because he was afraid to ask a stranger for directions. He had walked for an hour, arrived late and blamed the bus. “When you do not know a word or a way,” he wrote, “ask a question before the problem grows.” Malika laughed at the advice, then noticed a second line: the ticket was for the town library, where he had learned English as a young man.

That Saturday, she persuaded her mother to take her there. The library was smaller than she expected, but an elderly volunteer recognized the surname on the note. He showed Malika a shelf of old notebooks. Her grandfather had written unfamiliar words in the margins and added example sentences from conversations he heard at the market. Some spellings were wrong, and several pages were crossed out. Malika liked these mistakes more than the neat dictionary entries because they showed someone learning in real time.

The volunteer offered to let her borrow one notebook for a week. Malika chose the thinnest one and copied a phrase about asking for help into her own notebook. On the way home, the bus stopped at an unfamiliar street after a road closure. A passenger looked confused. This time Malika asked the driver which stop was nearest to the library. The answer saved them both a long walk.

For her class assignment, Malika wrote about the envelope, the notebook and the question she had asked on the bus. She concluded that an ordinary object can carry an unusual lesson, but only if someone is willing to open it.

When Brookside Secondary School replaced a section of its dark roof with a garden, the project began as a practical response to summer heat. The building’s top floor had become uncomfortable by early afternoon, and the air-conditioning system was working harder each year. Teachers proposed a green roof: a shallow layer of soil and hardy plants installed over a waterproof membrane. The school also added rain barrels and a small weather station so pupils could study the changes rather than simply admire the plants.

The first results were modest but measurable. On hot days, the roof surface beneath the plants was cooler than the exposed section. Classrooms directly below the garden warmed more slowly, although the effect varied with wind, cloud cover and how wet the soil was. The school therefore avoided claiming that the garden alone had solved its energy problem. Instead, science classes compared temperature readings across several months and discussed which other factors might explain the pattern.

Rainwater collection produced a second benefit. Water from the barrels was used for the garden, reducing the amount taken from the school supply during dry weeks. Pupils noticed that a heavy storm filled the barrels quickly, while a series of light showers did not. They used these observations to estimate water use and to consider why storage capacity matters in cities where paved surfaces send rain into drains rather than soil.

The project also changed how lessons were organized. Biology classes recorded plant growth, mathematics groups calculated averages, and English learners wrote short reports for families. A local horticulturist advised the school to choose native plants that could survive periods without watering. This advice challenged the assumption that a roof garden should look like a decorative park. The goal was resilience and learning, not a perfect display.

Brookside’s experience cannot be copied exactly everywhere. Roof strength, climate, maintenance budgets and access to water differ from school to school. The staff now share their measurements and mistakes with neighboring schools, emphasizing that a useful climate project begins with a local question, gathers evidence over time and remains honest about uncertainty.

questions.q: At gap G5, which sentence best prepares for a revision cycle?
questions.a: The criteria are unrelated to the learning goal.
questions.b: A final score is the only useful classroom evidence.
questions.c: Revision gives learners a chance to apply the advice to their work.
questions.d: This means teachers should stop reading student drafts.
questions.passage:
Teachers often return marked work with the intention of helping learners improve. Yet a page covered in corrections may leave a student unsure where to begin. Feedback becomes more useful when it points to a manageable next step. [G1]

A learner who knows the goal can compare a draft with clear success criteria. [G2] For example, a writing task might ask students to support one claim with evidence and explain how the evidence relates to it. [G3] The teacher can then comment on that feature before addressing every spelling choice. [G4] Students need time to act on the comments, not merely read them. [G5]

A short revision cycle makes feedback part of learning rather than a final judgement. This approach does not mean that accuracy is unimportant. It means that comments should be prioritized. When a class is practicing past-tense narratives, repeated errors with verb forms may deserve attention; during a debate unit, clarity of reasoning may matter more. A teacher can also ask learners to identify one strength and one question about their own work. Such reflection helps them take responsibility without pretending that they can diagnose every problem alone.

Over time, teachers can review patterns across student work and adjust instruction. If many learners misunderstand the same feature, the next lesson can address it directly. In this way, assessment information guides both the learner’s revision and the teacher’s planning.
